g11-mathematics-um6-t1.overview: Translation (slide): every point moves by the same vector. The matrix form with homogeneous coordinates, properties, and composing translations.
objectives: Describe a translation by its vector (h, k)
Apply translations to points and figures
Use the homogeneous matrix T = [1 0 h; 0 1 k; 0 0 1]
Compose translations (vectors add)
Find inverse translations (vector negated)
g11-mathematics-um6-t1.simple: A translation SLIDES every point the same distance in the same direction — the vector (h, k) is the instruction: 'move h right, k up'. Point rule: (x, y) → (x+h, y+k). Triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (0,3) translated by (2, −1) → (2,−1), (6,−1), (2,2): same shape, same orientation, new address. TRANSLATIONS ARE NOT 2×2 MATRIX MAPS on (x,y) — a slide doesn't fix the origin (linear maps always send 0→0), so we cheat with HOMOGENEOUS COORDINATES: write (x, y) as the 3-vector (x, y, 1) and use T = [1 0 h; 0 1 k; 0 0 1]. Multiply: [1 0 h; 0 1 k; 0 0 1]·(x, y, 1) = (x+h, y+k, 1) — the slide as a matrix product. Why bother? Matrices COMPOSE: two translations T(h₁,k₁) then T(h₂,k₂) = T(h₁+h₂, k₁+k₂) — the product matrix just adds the vectors (check by multiplying the matrices). Inverse: T(−h, −k) — slide back. Properties: translations preserve distance (isometries), angles, orientation, and map lines to parallel lines. Every rigid motion of the plane is a translation, rotation, reflection, or glide — this topic starts the catalogue.
g11-mathematics-um6-t1.detailed:
Homogeneous coordinates. The point (x, y) becomes the column (x, y, 1)ᵀ; the extra 1 is the 'affine flag' that lets constant shifts appear as matrix products (the h, k live in the third column). All plane transformations — slides, turns, flips, scalings, shears — become 3×3 matrices, and composition becomes multiplication. This is the coordinate system of computer graphics pipelines.

Structure. T(h,k) = I with the translation vector bolted into column 3. det T = 1 (triangular with 1s on the diagonal) — orientation-preserving, area-preserving (it's a rigid motion). The set of all translations is a group: identity T(0,0), inverse T(−h,−k), closure (sum of vectors), commutative (vector addition is!).

Composing with other maps. Rotate then translate: apply right-to-left — M = T·R acting on (x,y,1). Order matters: T·R ≠ R·T in general (translate-then-rotate swings the offset around). Reading a product matrix: the third column is where the origin went — for a pure translation it IS (h, k, 1); for a rotation+translation it's the translation part after the rotation.

Figure work. Translate a polygon: move each vertex, rejoin. A translation is determined by ONE point-image pair: if A maps to A′, the vector is AA→′ — every other point follows the same arrow. Conversely, matching any point to its image recovers the slide.

workedExamples.problem: Translate P(3, −2) by vector (−1, 5).
Verify with the homogeneous matrix: T(2, −1) applied to (4, 0).
A(1,1) maps to A′(5, −2). Give the translation and find B(0, 4)'s image.
Compose T(1, 2) followed by T(3, −1): single translation?
workedExamples.answer: T(4, 1) — matrix product confirms (multiply the two 3×3s)

workedExamples.problem: Triangle (0,0), (2,0), (0,1) translated by (−3, 2): new vertices and area?
workedExamples.answer: Vertices as above; area still 1 — translations are isometries

commonMistakes: Trying to write a translation as a 2×2 matrix — impossible (origin must move); use 3×3 homogeneous
Applying (x+h, y+k) to only some vertices of a figure
Order confusion in composition: T·R means rotate FIRST (right-to-left)
Forgetting the third coordinate stays 1 after multiplying
Reading the translation from the wrong column — it's column 3 of the 3×3
Thinking translation changes orientation — det = 1, it never does
applications: Computer graphics: moving sprites/camera pans (translation matrices)
Crystallography: lattice translations define crystal structure
Robotics: base-to-joint offsets in kinematic chains
Tiling & design: repeating patterns by translation vectors
g11-mathematics-um6-t1.summary: Translation = slide by (h, k): (x, y) → (x+h, y+k), a rigid motion preserving size, shape, and orientation. As a matrix it needs homogeneous coordinates: the 3×3 with (h, k) in column 3. Composing translations adds vectors; the inverse negates them; one point-image pair determines the whole slide. det = 1 — orientation and area preserved. The homogeneous trick is the gateway to writing EVERY plane transformation as a matrix product.

questions.q: The homogeneous translation matrix carries (h, k) in:
A translation can be written as a 2×2 matrix acting on (x, y).
A translation is determined by ___ point-image pair(s):
A(−2, 3) → A′(4, −1). Find the translation vector and image of B(1, 1).
Why can't a translation be a linear map on R²?
questions.explanation: Linear maps send 0 to 0 (L(0) = L(0·v) = 0·L(v)); a translation moves the origin by (h, k) ≠ 0 — so it's affine, not linear, which is exactly why the homogeneous 3×3 representation is needed

g11-mathematics-um6-t2.overview: Reflection (flip): mirror across a line. Matrix forms for the axes and y = x, the perpendicular-bisector construction, and orientation reversal (det = −1).
objectives: Reflect points in the x-axis, y-axis, and line y = x
Write the 2×2 reflection matrices
Construct reflections of figures (perpendicular bisector property)
Use det = −1 to identify reflections
Reflect in other lines (y = −x, vertical/horizontal lines x = a)
g11-mathematics-um6-t2.simple: A reflection FLIPS the plane over a mirror line: every point and its image sit on a perpendicular to the mirror, equidistant from it — the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of P P′→. THE FOUR CLASSROOM MIRRORS: x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y), matrix [1 0; 0 −1]; y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y), matrix [−1 0; 0 1]; line y = x: (x, y) → (y, x) — coordinates SWAP, matrix [0 1; 1 0]; line y = −x: (x, y) → (−y, −x), matrix [0 −1; −1 0]. Off-origin mirrors: reflect in x = a: (x, y) → (2a−x, y) (the mirror is the midpoint: (x + x′)/2 = a). Properties: reflections are ISOMETRIES (distances kept) but they REVERSE orientation — like turning a glove inside out; the determinant is −1 (compare translation/rotation: +1). Left hand ↔ right hand: a reflected figure can't be slid/rotated onto its original — that's orientation reversal you can hold. Composition surprise: two reflections in parallel lines = a TRANSLATION (by twice the gap); two reflections in intersecting lines = a ROTATION (by twice the angle) — flips build every other motion.
g11-mathematics-um6-t2.detailed:
Mirror-line formula. Reflection in the line through the origin at angle θ: matrix [cos 2θ sin 2θ; sin 2θ −cos 2θ]. Check: θ = 0 (x-axis) → [1 0; 0 −1] ✓; θ = 45° (y = x) → [0 1; 1 0] ✓. The doubled angle appears because reflecting twice across lines at θ and φ rotates by 2(φ−θ).

Construction. To reflect a figure: drop perpendiculars from each vertex to the mirror, extend equally beyond — or use the coordinate rules for standard mirrors. Points ON the mirror are fixed (their own images) — the mirror line is the fixed-point set.

Off-origin mirrors. x = a: (x,y) → (2a−x, y); y = b: (x,y) → (x, 2b−y). General line: translate the mirror to the origin, reflect with the θ-formula, translate back — the homogeneous 3×3 version composes these three steps into one matrix.

Orientation & determinants. det = −1 characterizes reflections (and glide reflections) among isometries: the image of a counterclockwise triangle runs clockwise. Algebraically the reflection matrix has eigenvalues +1 (mirror direction, fixed) and −1 (perpendicular direction, flipped) — trace 0 for through-origin mirrors. The mirror line is the +1 eigenspace — an eigenvector reading of the geometry.

workedExamples.problem: Reflect (3, −2) in: (a) x-axis, (b) y-axis, (c) y = x.
Reflect (5, 1) in the line x = 2.
Use the θ-matrix to reflect (0, 1) in the 30° line.
workedExamples.answer: (√3/2, −1/2) — the unit vector at −30°: mirror of 90° across 30°

workedExamples.problem: Triangle (0,0), (2,0), (0,1) reflected in y = x. Show orientation flips.
Reflect the line y = 2x + 1 in the x-axis.
workedExamples.answer: y = −2x − 1 — slope and intercept both flip

commonMistakes: y = x reflection: negating instead of SWAPPING coordinates
Off-origin mirror: using −x instead of 2a − x (forgetting the shift)
Calling reflections orientation-preserving — det = −1 flips
θ-matrix: writing cos θ instead of cos 2θ
Reflecting only vertices and forgetting edges follow automatically
Confusing y = −x rule (−y, −x) with y = x rule (y, x)
applications: Optics & mirrors: image construction in plane mirrors
Computer graphics: billboard flips and reflection matrices
g11-mathematics-um6-t2.summary: Reflection flips the plane over a mirror line — the perpendicular bisector of every point-image pair; mirror points stay fixed. The four standard rules: x-axis (x,−y), y-axis (−x,y), y=x (swap), y=−x (swap+negate); general through-origin mirror uses the 2θ matrix; off-origin mirrors shift by 2a. Isometry with det = −1: orientation reverses (left hand ↔ right hand). Two parallel mirrors = translation; two angled mirrors = rotation — reflections generate the whole motion catalogue.

questions.q: Reflection in y = x sends (a, b) to:
A reflected figure can always be rotated back onto the original.
Two reflections in parallel lines give a translation.
The mirror line consists of the ___ points of the reflection:
Reflect A(1,2), B(3,2) in the x-axis and give AB′... A′B′ length.
Explain why your mirror image raises the opposite hand.
questions.explanation: A mirror reflection reverses the axis perpendicular to it (front-back), which flips the handedness of the coordinate frame — a raised right hand maps to the image's right side appearing on your left: the reflection is an orientation-reversing isometry (det −1), so left and right trade places

g11-mathematics-um6-t3.overview: Rotation (turn): every point spins about a center through a fixed angle. The 2×2 rotation matrix, the 90°/180° rules, direction conventions, and rotation composition.
objectives: Rotate points about the origin by 90°, 180°, 270° by rule
Use the general rotation matrix [cosθ −sinθ; sinθ cosθ]
Rotate about a center other than the origin
Compose rotations (angles add) and invert (negate)
Identify rotations by det = +1 and fixed center
g11-mathematics-um6-t3.simple: A rotation TURNS the plane about a fixed center through an angle — counterclockwise positive by convention. ORIGIN RULES (memorize): 90° CCW: (x, y) → (−y, x); 180°: (x, y) → (−x, −y); 270° CCW (= 90° CW): (x, y) → (y, −x). GENERAL ANGLE θ: matrix R(θ) = [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ] — multiply by (x, y). Check: θ = 90° gives [0 −1; 1 0] → (−y, x) ✓. The first column is where (1,0) lands, the second where (0,1) lands — read any rotation off the axes' fates. OFF-ORIGIN center C: slide C to the origin, rotate, slide back: P → C + R(θ)(P − C). Example: rotate (4, 1) about (1, 2) by 90°: (4,1)−(1,2) = (3,−1) → rotate → (1, 3) → add C → (2, 5). Properties: rotations are isometries with det = +1 (orientation PRESERVED — a turned glove still fits the same hand); the center is the only fixed point (180° about C: C is midpoint of every PP′→). Composition: R(α) then R(β) = R(α+β) — angles add, matrices multiply (the trig identities hide in the product!). Inverse: R(−θ). Every orientation-preserving isometry is a rotation (or translation) — the next topic glues these together.
g11-mathematics-um6-t3.detailed:
Matrix derivation. The unit circle point (cos φ, sin φ) rotates to (cos(φ+θ), sin(φ+θ)); expanding with addition formulas gives x′ = x cos θ − y sin θ, y′ = x sin θ + y cos θ — the matrix. Columns = images of i and j: i → (cos θ, sin θ) (the angle's terminal point), j → (−sin θ, cos θ) (i rotated 90° more).

Center mechanics. P′ = C + R(P − C): the vector from the center rotates, the center anchors. Homogeneous 3×3 version composes T(C)·R(θ)·T(−C) into one matrix — the graphics-pipeline way. 180° special: P′ = 2C − P — the center is the midpoint of PP′→ (point symmetry).

Identification. det = +1 + a fixed point ⇒ rotation (about that point); det = +1 + no fixed point ⇒ translation; det = −1 ⇒ reflection or glide. Given a 2×2 orthogonal matrix with det 1, read θ from cos θ = (a+d)/2 — the trace encodes the angle.

Composition & group. R(α)R(β) = R(α+β) — the rotation matrices form a group (circle group SO(2)); powers: R(θ)ⁿ = R(nθ) — repeated turns multiply. Rotations about DIFFERENT centers compose to a rotation (angles add) or a translation (if total angle = 0 mod 360°) — the center-shift is the interesting part.

keyTerms.def: the fixed point of the turn

workedExamples.problem: Rotate (2, 5) by 90° CCW about the origin.

workedExamples.answer: (½, √3/2) — the unit circle at 60°, as it must be

workedExamples.problem: Rotate (4, 1) about C(1, 2) through 90° CCW.
180° rotation maps A(1, 3) to A′(5, −1). Find the center.
Rotate 30° then 45°: single matrix?
workedExamples.answer: R(75°) — the product of the two matrices equals it (trig identities)

commonMistakes: Clockwise vs counterclockwise: the standard matrix is CCW; CW = use −θ
90° rule written as (y, −x) — that's 270°; 90° CCW is (−y, x)
Off-origin: rotating the POSITION vector instead of the vector from the CENTER
Forgetting to add the center back after rotating about the shifted origin
Reading the matrix rows instead of COLUMNS as the axis images
Assuming the center must be inside the figure — it can be anywhere
applications: Computer graphics: object orientation (rotation matrices everywhere)
Robotics: joint angles are rotations about axes
Navigation: heading changes as rotations of the velocity vector
Physics: angular motion, polarization rotation of light
g11-mathematics-um6-t3.summary: Rotation turns the plane about a center by angle θ (CCW positive): origin rules (90°: (−y,x), 180°: (−x,−y), 270°: (y,−x)) and the general matrix [cosθ −sinθ; sinθ cosθ] whose columns are the axes' images. Off-origin: P′ = C + R(P−C); 180° makes C the midpoint of PP′→. Isometry with det = +1 (orientation kept); composition adds angles; inverse negates. Rotations + reflections + translations tile the plane's isometry catalogue — the next topic completes it.

questions.q: R(θ)'s first column is the image of:
A rotation about the origin fixes exactly one point.
Explain why the rotation matrix's columns are perpendicular unit vectors.
questions.explanation: Rotation preserves lengths and angles, so the images of the orthonormal basis i, j stay orthonormal — columns of length 1 (cos²+sin²) meeting at 90° (their dot product cosθ·(−sinθ) + sinθ·cosθ = 0); such matrices are orthogonal with det ±1, and +1 picks the rotation

g11-mathematics-um6-t4.overview: Applications of transformations: compositions (glide reflections, rototranslations), symmetry groups of figures, tessellations, and identifying a transformation from a figure pair.
objectives: Compose transformations via matrix products (right-to-left)
Identify a transformation from a figure and its image
Classify symmetries of figures (rotational, reflectional)
Explain glide reflections and their matrix form
Apply transformations to tessellation and design
g11-mathematics-um6-t4.simple: Put the pieces together. COMPOSITION: do transformations in sequence — multiply their matrices, applying RIGHTMOST first: (T·R)(P) = T(R(P)). Rotate 90° then translate (2,0): single 3×3 product does both. IDENTIFYING from a figure pair: (1) check distances — preserved? then isometry; (2) check orientation — same? rotation or translation; reversed? reflection or glide; (3) find fixed points — a center? rotation about it; none + parallel segments? translation; a mirror line of fixed points? reflection; none of these with reversed orientation? GLIDE (reflect + slide along the mirror). SYMMETRY GROUPS: all transformations mapping a figure ONTO itself. Square: 8 symmetries (4 rotations 0/90/180/270 + 4 reflections) — the dihedral group D₄; rectangle: 4; equilateral triangle: 6; circle: infinitely many. Letters are mini-exams: A has one vertical mirror; S has 180° rotation only; H has both mirrors + rotation; N only rotation. TESSELLATIONS: the 17 wallpaper patterns are all combinations of translations, rotations, reflections, glides — Ethiopian tile and textile geometry runs on this. The big theorem: every plane isometry is exactly one of translation, rotation, reflection, or glide reflection — four families, all matrices.
g11-mathematics-um6-t4.detailed:
Composition algebra. In homogeneous 3×3 form, any isometry is M = [A t; 0 1] with A orthogonal (2×2) and t the translation part. Products: (A₁ t₁)(A₂ t₂) = (A₁A₂, A₁t₂ + t₁) — the second rotation happens in the first's frame. Order matters: R·T ≠ T·R (rotate-then-slide vs slide-then-rotate give different results — the translation vector itself rotates in R·T).

Classification theorem. Isometry types by (det A, fixed points): det +1, fixed point → rotation; det +1, no fixed point (t ≠ 0 in the invariant direction) → translation; det −1, fixed line → reflection; det −1, no fixed points → glide reflection (the square of a glide is a translation along the mirror — detectable: g² = T ≠ identity while g ≠ T).

Symmetry groups. Finite figures: cyclic Cₙ (rotations only, e.g. pinwheel) or dihedral Dₙ (rotations + n mirrors, e.g. regular n-gon). Counting: a regular n-gon has 2n symmetries. Composition tables: D₃ (triangle) is the smallest non-abelian group — reflection order matters, a concrete feel for non-commutativity.

Design applications. Wallpaper groups: 7 frieze (strip) + 17 plane groups classify all repeating patterns by which of the four isometry types appear. Escher tessellations: a tile modified by a glide/rotation still tiles. Ethiopian patterns (tibeb borders, gabi stripes): frieze groups — identify mirrors, half-turns, glides along the band.

workedExamples.problem: Rotate (1, 0) by 90° CCW, then translate by (0, 2). Single matrix product?
Triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,2) maps to (1,0), (0,0), (1,2). Which isometry?
workedExamples.substitution: edges 1, 2, √5 in both → isometry; orientation reversed (CCW→CW) → reflection or glide; rule (x,y)→(1−x,y) fits all three pairs; fixed line x = 0.5
workedExamples.answer: Reflection in the vertical line x = 0.5

workedExamples.problem: List the symmetries of a rectangle (non-square).
workedExamples.substitution: identity, 180° rotation about center, reflection in each of the 2 midlines
workedExamples.answer: 4 symmetries (no 90° turns, no diagonal mirrors — those break the rectangle)

workedExamples.problem: Which letters have exactly one reflection symmetry: A, B, C, N, S, X?
workedExamples.substitution: A: vertical ✓; B: horizontal ✓; C: horizontal ✓; N: none (rotation only); S: none (rotation only); X: two mirrors
workedExamples.answer: A, B, C each have exactly one mirror

workedExamples.problem: Show a glide (reflect in x-axis + translate (1,0)) squared is a translation.
workedExamples.answer: g² = translation by (2, 0) — the signature of a glide

commonMistakes: Composing left-to-right — matrix products apply the RIGHTMOST transformation first
Assuming composition commutes — R·T ≠ T·R generally
Calling every orientation-reversal a reflection — check for glides (no fixed points)
Square symmetries counted as 4 — it's 8 (add the 4 reflections)
Glide detection: forgetting the glide's slide must be PARALLEL to its mirror
Confusing symmetry of a figure with symmetry of its motion (the figure maps to ITSELF)
applications: Crystallography: 230 space groups classify all crystal symmetries
Art & design: tessellations, textile and tile patterns (tibeb friezes)
Robotics & animation: chained joint transforms are compositions
Image processing: registration = finding the composition that aligns scans
g11-mathematics-um6-t4.summary: Transformations compose: multiply homogeneous matrices, rightmost first — order matters. Every plane isometry is one of four families: translation, rotation, reflection, glide reflection, diagnosed by distance-preservation, orientation (det sign), and fixed points. Symmetry groups catalogue a figure's self-maps (regular n-gon: Dₙ, 2n elements; letters as quick tests). Repeating patterns — friezes, wallpapers, Ethiopian textile bands — are these groups made visible. Four isometries, one matrix algebra, infinite design.

questions.q: Orientation-reversing isometry with NO fixed points:
Two rotations compose to a rotation (or translation).
Every transformation is a symmetry of every figure.
The regular hexagon's symmetry group has ___ elements:
Why is the set of a figure's symmetries always a group?
questions.explanation: Composing two self-maps gives a self-map (closure); the identity map is a symmetry; every symmetry is invertible (isometries are bijective, inverse is also a self-map); associativity holds for all maps — the four group axioms check automatically
